title: Egyptian grammar
about: Only what Egyptian Arabic does differently from Modern Standard Arabic, in 16 short lessons: the Cairo sounds, no case endings, the pronouns, the b- present, “right now”, the future with ha-, the past endings, saying “not” with ma…sh and mish, the question words, da, di and dōl, bitāʿ, illi, “want” and “must”, “there is”, numbers and “if”. It builds on the Arabic grammar course: whatever works as in MSA is left out. The examples are everyday Cairo speech, vowelled the way Cairenes say them, with a reading in Latin letters.

lessons.title: Say it the Cairo way
lessons.summary: Five letters and two vowel pairs sound different in Cairo. Learn them once, and thousands of MSA words become Egyptian.
lessons.topic: {{ق}} said ʾ, {{ج}} said g, {{ث}} {{ذ}} {{ظ}} said t/s, d/z, ḍ/ẓ; ay → ē, aw → ō

dialog.tr: What would you like to drink?

blocks.p: You know these words from MSA: {{قَهْوَة}} “coffee”, {{جَمِيل}} “beautiful”, {{جِدًّا}} “very”. Egyptians write them the same way but **say** them differently, as the readings show: {{قَهْوَة|ʾahwa}} starts with a catch in the throat instead of q, and {{جَمِيل|gamīl}} with a g as in “go”.

table: ʾ, a catch in the throat (the break in “uh-oh”)
t in everyday words, s in learned ones
d in everyday words, z in learned ones
ḍ in everyday words, ẓ in learned ones

blocks.p: In writing, Egyptians usually spell the everyday words the way they say them: {{تَلَاتَة}} for {{ثَلَاثَة}}, {{دَهَب}} for {{ذَهَب}}, {{ضَهْر}} for {{ظَهْر}}. Learned words (from school, the news, religion) keep their MSA spelling and only change the sound: {{ثَقَافَة|saqāfa}}.
**Two vowel pairs shrink**: ay becomes a long ē and aw a long ō. {{بَيْت|bēt}} house, {{عَيْن|ʿēn}} eye, {{يَوْم|yōm}} day, {{لَوْن|lōn}} colour. They are written as in MSA.

blocks.tip: A few words keep their q even in Cairo, mostly religious or formal ones: {{الْقُرْآن|il-qurʾān}}. And everyday Cairenes call their city {{مَصْر|maṣr}}, the same word as Egypt.

mistakes.why: Everyday words with {{ث}} are said, and usually written, with {{ت}} in Egyptian: {{تَلَات|talat}}.

practice.why: {{ق}} is a catch in the throat in Cairo: ʾalb.

practice.q: Your turn: order a drink in a Cairo café, the Cairo way.

answers.t: قَهْوَة مِن غَيْر سُكَّر، لَوْ سَمَحْتِي.
answers.r: ʾahwa min ghēr sukkar, law samaḥti.
answers.tr: A coffee without sugar, please. (to a woman)

lessons.title: Drop the endings: one, two and more
lessons.summary: No case endings, no -un, and a dual only on nouns: here Egyptian is simpler than MSA.
lessons.topic: no case endings or {{ـٌ}}; the dual {{ـَيْن}} on nouns only; plural verbs and adjectives for two; no feminine plural

goal.tr: I've got two sisters and one brother.

dialog.tr: Have you got brothers or sisters?
Yes, two sisters and one brother.
And is your big sister married?
Yes, and she's got two little boys.

blocks.p: **No endings.** Egyptian never says the case endings -u, -a, -i or the -un of MSA: {{كِتَاب|kitāb}}, never kitābun; {{فِي الْبَيْت|fi l-bēt}}, never fī l-bayti. A word sounds the same whether it is the subject, the object or after a preposition.

**Two of something**: nouns take {{ـَيْن|-ēn}}, never {{ـَان|-ān}}: {{يَوْمَيْن|yomēn}} two days, {{أُخْتَيْن|ukhtēn}} two sisters. A word ending in {{ة}} changes it to {{ت}}: {{سَاعَة|sāʿa}}, {{سَاعْتَيْن|saʿtēn}} two hours. Verbs, adjectives and pronouns have no dual: two people are simply plural.

table: the two of them are tired

blocks.p: There is no feminine plural for verbs, adjectives or pronouns either: a group of women takes the same plural as any group.

ex.tr: Those two girls are my friends.
My brother and his wife are tired.

mistakes.why: The Egyptian dual ends in {{ـَيْن|-ēn}}, never {{ـَان|-ān}}.
Only nouns have a dual. The adjective for two people is plural: {{تَعْبَانِين}}.

practice.tr: I stayed in Cairo for two days.

practice.why: -ēn, the {{ة}} becomes {{ت}}, and nothing after it: saʿtēn.
No dual for adjectives: two people take the plural, {{مَبْسُوطِين}}.

practice.q: Your turn: say how many brothers and sisters you have, or how many days you're staying.

answers.tr: I've got one brother and two sisters.
I'll stay here just two days.

lessons.title: Say we, you all, they, and my, your, his
lessons.summary: The pronouns {{إِحْنَا}}, {{إِنْتُو}}, {{هُمَّا}}, and the endings that differ: {{ـُه}} “his”, {{ـكُو}} “your (all)”.

goal.tr: We're from Egypt, and where are you all from?

dialog.t: إِحْنَا مِن أَلْمَانْيَا، وِدُول صُحَابْنَا مِن فَرَنْسَا.
dialog.r: iḥna min almanya, wi-dōl ṣuḥabna min faransa.
dialog.tr: We're from Germany, and these are our friends from France.

dialog.t: أَهْلًا بِيكُو! بَيْتْكُو قُرَيِّب مِن هِنَا؟
dialog.r: ahlan bīku! betku ʾurayyib min hina?
dialog.tr: Welcome! Is your place near here?
Yes, our place is in Zamalek.

blocks.p: The pronouns that differ from MSA: {{إِحْنَا|iḥna}} we (MSA {{نَحْنُ}}), {{إِنْتُو|intu}} you all (MSA {{أَنْتُمْ}}), {{هُمَّا|humma}} they (MSA {{هُمْ}}), and {{إِنْتِي|inti}} you, to a woman. {{أَنَا|ana}}, {{إِنْتَ|inta}}, {{هُوَّ|huwwa}} and {{هِيَّ|hiyya}} are the MSA words with Cairo vowels. There is no dual ({{أَنْتُمَا}}) and no feminine plural ({{أَنْتُنَّ}}, {{هُنَّ}}): {{إِنْتُو}} and {{هُمَّا}} are for any group.

The endings for “my, your, his…” are the MSA ones without their last vowels, with two to learn: **his** is {{ـُه|-u}} (written {{ه}}, said u: {{بَيْتُه|bētu}}), and **your (all)** is {{ـكُو|-ku}} or {{ـكُم|-kum}}. The same endings mean “me, you, him…” after a verb: {{شُفْتُه|shuftu}} I saw him.

mistakes.why: “We” is {{إِحْنَا}} in Egyptian; {{نَحْنُ}} sounds like the news.
Egyptian has no feminine plural: {{هُمَّا}} is “they” for women too.

practice.q: A neighbour greets you and your friends. Choose your replies.
How do you ask a woman “Are you Egyptian?”
Your turn: say where you and your family are from, and where they live.

answers.t: إِحْنَا مِن كَنَدَا، وِأَهْلِي عَايْشِين فِي تُورُنْتُو.
answers.r: iḥna min kanada, wi-ahli ʿayshīn fi toronto.
answers.tr: We're from Canada, and my family lives in Toronto.

lessons.title: Say what you do every day
lessons.summary: Egyptian present verbs take {{بِـ}}: {{بَشْرَب قَهْوَة كُلّ يَوْم}} “I drink coffee every day”. Without it, the verb follows words like “want” and “must”.
lessons.topic: {{بِـ}} + the present: {{بَكْتِب}}, {{بِتِكْتِب}}, {{بِيِكْتِب}}, {{بِنِكْتِب}}, {{بِيِكْتِبُوا}}; the plain present after {{عَايِز}}, {{لَازِم}}, {{مُمْكِن}}

dialog.t: بَشْتَغَل فِي بَنْك فِي وِسْط الْبَلَد.
dialog.r: bashtaghal fi bank fi wisṭ il-balad.
dialog.tr: I work at a bank downtown.
And how do you get to work?
I take the metro every day.

blocks.p: In MSA the present is {{أَكْتُبُ}}, {{يَكْتُبُ}}. Egyptian puts {{بِـ|bi-}} in front for anything that happens regularly or is going on: {{بِيِكْتِب|biyiktib}} he writes, he's writing. With “I”, the {{أَ}} merges into it: {{بَكْتِب|baktib}} I write.
The plural ends in {{ـُوا|-u}}, without the {{ن}} of MSA, and the vowels are often i: {{يِكْتِب|yiktib}}, not yaktubu.
**Without {{بِـ}}**: after {{عَايِز}} “want”, {{لَازِم}} “must”, {{مُمْكِن}} “can” and {{عَشَان}} “so that”, the verb takes no {{بِـ}} and no {{أَنْ}}: {{عَايِز أَكْتِب|ʿāyiz aktib}} I want to write.

ex.tr: Do you like koshary? (to a woman)

practice.q: Your friends, a group, speak Arabic. Which is Egyptian?
Your turn: say three things you do every day.

answers.t: بَصْحَى بَدْرِي، وِبَشْرَب شَاي، وِبَرُوح الشُّغْل.
answers.r: baṣḥa badri, wi-bashrab shāy, wi-barūḥ ish-shughl.
answers.tr: I get up early, drink tea and go to work.

lessons.title: Say what's happening right now
lessons.summary: {{بِـ}} also means “right now”; {{عَمَّال}} says “keeps on”; and words like {{رَايِح}} “going” and {{عَارِف}} “knowing” do the work of a verb.

goal.tr: I'm on my way to work now.

dialog.tr: You keep being late every day!

blocks.p: {{بِـ}} covers both “I do” and “I'm doing”: {{بِتِعْمِل إِيه؟|bitiʿmil ē?}} is “What are you doing?” as well as “What do you do?”. The situation tells which.

**Keeps on**: {{عَمَّال|ʿammāl}} before a present verb says something goes on and on: {{عَمَّال يِتْكَلِّم|ʿammāl yitkallim}} he keeps talking. It agrees: {{عَمَّالَة|ʿammāla}} for a woman, {{عَمَّالِين|ʿammalīn}} for a group.

**Doer words** (the {{فَاعِل}} pattern of MSA) are used far more than in MSA, as the verb itself, for moving, knowing and staying: {{أَنَا رَايِح|ana rāyiḥ}} I'm going, {{هِيَّ جَايَّة|hiyya gayya}} she's coming, {{مِش عَارِف|mish ʿārif}} I don't know, {{فَاكِر؟|fākir?}} remember?. They change like adjectives:

ex.tr: Where are you going? (to a woman)

mistakes.why: Egyptian uses {{رَايِح}} “going” for where you're headed, with no {{إِلَى}} before the place.
Doer words agree like adjectives: {{رَايْحَة}} for a woman.

options: only “What do you do (for a living)?”

practice.q: A friend calls you. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: OK, what are you doing now?

practice.q: A man says “I don't know”. What does he say?
Your turn: say where you're going today, and what someone near you keeps doing.

answers.t: أَنَا رَايِح السُّوق، وِأَخُويَا عَمَّال يِتْفَرَّج عَلَى الْمَاتْش.
answers.r: ana rāyiḥ is-sūʾ, wi-akhūya ʿammāl yitfarrag ʿala l-matsh.
answers.tr: I'm going to the market, and my brother keeps watching the match.

lessons.title: Talk about your plans
lessons.summary: The future is {{هَـ}} in front of the present: {{هَرُوح بُكْرَة}} “I'll go tomorrow”.

goal.tr: I'll go to the seaside tomorrow.

dialog.tr: What are you going to do on holiday?
Nice! How long will you stay?
A week, and we won't work at all!

blocks.p: MSA has {{سَـ}} and {{سَوْفَ}}. Egyptian puts {{هَـ|ha-}} (some people say {{حَـ|ḥa-}}) in front of the present, in place of {{بِـ}}: {{هَكْتِب|haktib}} I'll write, {{هَيِكْتِب|hayiktib}} he'll write, {{هَنِكْتِب|haniktib}} we'll write.
**Won't**: put {{مِش|mish}} in front: {{مِش هَرُوح|mish harūḥ}} I won't go. (The lesson on “not” shows the other way of saying it.)

ex.tr: Will you come to the party?
The weather's going to be hot.

mistakes.why: {{هَـ}} takes the place of {{بِـ}}: never both.

practice.tr: We'll go to Alexandria next week.
I won't go to work tomorrow.
Will you come to the party?

practice.q: A friend asks {{إِنْتَ فِين؟}}. You're on your way. You say…
practice.why: On your way now: the doer word {{جَاي}}.

practice.q: Your turn: say three things you'll do this weekend.

answers.t: هَنَام كِتِير، وِهَقَابِل صُحَابِي، وِهَتْفَرَّج عَلَى فِيلْم.
answers.r: hanām kitīr, wi-haʾābil ṣuḥābi, wi-hatfarrag ʿala film.
answers.tr: I'll sleep a lot, meet my friends and watch a film.

lessons.title: Say what you did
lessons.summary: The past works as in MSA, with shorter endings: {{كَتَبْت}} “I wrote, you wrote”, {{كَتَبُوا}} “they wrote”.

goal.tr: Yesterday I went to the cinema with my friends.

dialog.tr: I went to the cinema. And you?
He and his friends played football.

blocks.p: The past is the MSA past without its final vowels. **I** and **you (man)** are the same: {{كَتَبْت|katabt}}. **You (woman)** adds -i: {{كَتَبْتِي|katabti}}. **She** is {{كَتَبِت|katabit}}. **We** {{كَتَبْنَا|katabna}}, **you all** {{كَتَبْتُوا|katabtu}}, **they** {{كَتَبُوا|katabu}}. There are no dual or feminine plural forms.

Many verbs that are {{فَعِلَ}} in MSA are said with i…i in Cairo: {{شِرِب|shirib}} he drank, {{فِهِم|fihim}} he understood, {{لِعِب|liʿib}} he played. Their endings are the same: {{شِرِبْت|shiribt}}, {{لِعْبُوا|liʿbu}}.

ex.tr: I drank tea and ate a sandwich.
Where did you all park the car?

practice.tr: Yesterday she went to the cinema.
What did you eat? (to a woman)

practice.q: “Yesterday I went, tomorrow I'll go.” Which is right?
Your turn: say three things you did yesterday.

answers.t: صِحِيت بَدْرِي، وِرُحْت الشُّغْل، وِاتْعَشَّيْت مَعَ أَهْلِي.
answers.r: ṣiḥīt badri, wi-ruḥt ish-shughl, wi-tʿashshēt maʿa ahli.
answers.tr: I got up early, went to work and had dinner with my family.

lessons.title: Say no and not
lessons.summary: Two ways to say “not”: {{مَا…ش}} round a verb ({{مَاشُفْتُوش}} “I didn't see him”) and {{مِش}} before everything else.
lessons.topic: {{مَا…ش}} with past and present verbs and with {{عَنْد}}; {{مِش}} with the future, doer words, adjectives and nouns; {{مَفِيش}}

goal.tr: I don't know, I haven't seen him today.

dialog.tr: No, and he isn't answering the phone.

blocks.p: MSA has {{لَا}}, {{لَمْ}}, {{لَنْ}}, {{مَا}} and {{لَيْسَ}}. Egyptian has two. **{{مَا…ش}}** wraps round a verb: {{مَا|ma-}} in front, {{ـْش|-sh}} at the end, written as one word: {{شُفْت}} → {{مَاشُفْتِش|mashuftish}} I didn't see; {{بَعْرَف}} → {{مَبَعْرَفْش|mabaʿrafsh}} I don't know.

An ending for “him, it, me” comes before the {{ش}}: {{شُفْتُه}} I saw him → {{مَاشُفْتُوش|mashuftūsh}} I didn't see him. {{ش}} also goes on {{عَنْد}} and {{فِيه}}: {{مَعَنْدِيش|maʿandīsh}} I haven't got, {{مَفِيش|mafīsh}} there isn't.

**{{مِش|mish}}** goes before everything that isn't a plain verb: the future ({{مِش هَرُوح}} I won't go), doer words ({{مِش عَارِف}} I don't know), adjectives ({{مِش غَالِي}} not expensive), nouns and places ({{مِش هِنَا}} not here). It does the work of MSA {{لَيْسَ}} and more.

blocks.tip: Telling someone not to do something works the same way, on the present without {{بِـ}}: {{مَتِقْلَقْش|matiʾlaʾsh}} don't worry, {{مَتْرُوحِيش|matruḥīsh}} don't go (to a woman).

mistakes.why: A plain verb takes {{مَا…ش}} round it, not {{مِش}}.

practice.q: A waiter asks you things. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: OK, would you like anything else?

practice.q: How do you say “We won't go”?
Your turn: say two things you don't like and one thing you didn't do yesterday.

answers.t: مَبَحِبِّش الزَّحْمَة وَلَا الدَّوْشَة، وِامْبَارِح مَارُحْتِش الشُّغْل.
answers.r: mabaḥibbish iz-zaḥma wala d-dawsha, wi-mbāriḥ maruḥtish ish-shughl.
answers.tr: I don't like crowds or noise, and yesterday I didn't go to work.

lessons.title: Ask who, what, where and when
lessons.summary: Egyptian question words are new words, and they like the end of the question: {{اسْمَك إِيه؟}} “What's your name?”

goal.tr: What's your name? And where are you from?

dialog.tr: Zamalek. When will we get there?
And how much is the fare?

blocks.p: The question words of MSA are replaced, and most of them go **where the answer would be**, often at the end: MSA {{مَا اسْمُكَ؟}}, Egyptian {{اسْمَك إِيه؟|ismak ē?}}, “your name is what?”; {{إِنْتَ رَايِح فِين؟|inta rāyiḥ fēn?}}, “you're going where?”.

{{لِيه}} and {{إِزَّاي}} often start the question; the others like the end. A yes-or-no question is just a sentence said with a rising voice: {{إِنْتَ مَصْرِي؟|inta maṣri?}}. Egyptian has no {{هَلْ}}.

ex.tr: How do I get to Tahrir?

mistakes.why: Egyptian has no {{هَلْ}}: just raise your voice.

practice.why: The past for “you all”, {{وِصِلْتُوا}}, and {{إِمْتَى}} at the end.

practice.q: Your turn: ask a new friend three questions.

answers.t: اسْمَك إِيه؟ إِنْتَ مِنِين؟ بِتِشْتَغَل فِين؟
answers.r: ismak ē? inta minēn? bitishtaghal fēn?
answers.tr: What's your name? Where are you from? Where do you work?

lessons.title: Point at this one and that one
lessons.summary: {{دَه}}, {{دِي}} and {{دُول}} mean both “this” and “that”, and they come after the noun: {{الْكِتَاب دَه}}.

goal.tr: I want this shirt, not that one.

blocks.p: MSA has {{هَذَا}} and {{ذَلِكَ}}, {{هَذِهِ}} and {{تِلْكَ}}. Egyptian has one set for near and far: {{دَه|da}} for a masculine word, {{دِي|di}} for a feminine word and for things in the plural, {{دُول|dōl}} for people in the plural.

With “the”, it comes **after** the noun: {{الْكِتَاب دَه|il-kitāb da}} this book, {{الْبِنْت دِي|il-bint di}} this girl, {{الْكُتُب دِي|il-kutub di}} these books. At the start of a sentence it means “this is”: {{دَه كِتَابِي|da kitābi}} this is my book.

table: feminine, and things in the plural

ex.tr: This is the best restaurant around here.

mistakes.why: For “this book”, {{دَه}} goes after the noun. {{دَه الْكِتَاب}} means “this is the book”.

practice.why: After the noun: {{الْكِتَاب دَه}}. ({{دَه كِتَاب}} is “this is a book”.)

practice.q: In a shop, ask “How much is this?” about a bag ({{شَنْطَة}}, feminine).
Your turn: point at three things around you and say something about each.

answers.t: الْكُبَّايَة دِي فَاضْيَة، وِالْكُرْسِي دَه مُرِيح.
answers.r: il-kubbāya di faḍya, wi-l-kursi da murīḥ.
answers.tr: This glass is empty, and this chair is comfortable.

lessons.title: Say whose it is with {{بِتَاع}}
lessons.summary: Besides the endings you know, Egyptian says “my, your” with {{بِتَاع}}: {{الْعَرَبِيَّة بِتَاعْتِي}} “my car”.

blocks.p: You can say {{عَرَبِيتِي|ʿarabiti}} “my car” with an ending, as in MSA. But Egyptians very often say {{الْعَرَبِيَّة بِتَاعْتِي|il-ʿarabiyya btaʿti}}, “the car belonging to me”. {{بِتَاع}} comes after a noun with “the”, and takes an ending or another noun: {{بِتَاع أَخُويَا|bitāʿ akhūya}} my brother's.

It agrees with the thing owned: {{بِتَاع|bitāʿ}} for a masculine word, {{بِتَاعِة|bitāʿit}} for a feminine word and for things in the plural ({{بِتَاعْت|bitaʿt-}} before an ending), {{بِتُوع|bitūʿ}} for people in the plural. On its own it means “mine, yours”: {{دَه بِتَاعِي|da btāʿi}} this is mine.
{{بِتَاع}} is for things you own, especially long or foreign words ({{الْمُوبَايِل بِتَاعِي}}). Family and the body keep the ending: {{أُمِّي}} my mother, never {{الْأُمّ بِتَاعْتِي}}.

practice.q: “Is this yours?”, about a pen ({{قَلَم}}), to a man:
Your turn: say whose some things near you are.

answers.t: الْمُوبَايِل دَه بِتَاعِي، وِالشَّنْطَة دِي بِتَاعِة أُخْتِي.
answers.r: il-mobāyil da btāʿi, wi-sh-shanṭa di btaʿit ukhti.
answers.tr: This phone is mine, and this bag is my sister's.

lessons.title: Say “the one who…” with {{اللِّي}}
lessons.topic: {{اللِّي}} for who, which, that and what

goal.tr: Where's the book I bought yesterday?

dialog.tr: Who's the girl who was with you?
That's Salma, who works with me.
Oh, the one you told me about?

blocks.p: MSA changes the word: {{الَّذِي}}, {{الَّتِي}}, {{اللَّذَانِ}}, {{الَّذِينَ}}… Egyptian has one word for all of them, {{اللِّي|illi}}, and it never changes: {{الرَّاجِل اللِّي|ir-rāgil illi}}, {{السِّتّ اللِّي|is-sitt illi}}, {{النَّاس اللِّي|in-nās illi}}.

As in MSA, when the thing talked about is the object, the verb after {{اللِّي}} takes an ending for it: {{الْفِيلْم اللِّي شُفْتُه|il-film illi shuftu}} the film (that) I saw (it). On its own, {{اللِّي}} means “what” or “the one who”: {{اللِّي فَات مَات|illi fāt māt}} what's past is dead (let bygones be bygones).

ex.tr: Murad's the one who told me.
This is the restaurant I love.
The people who came yesterday are nice.
Where are the papers that were here?

mistakes.tr: the girl who works with me

mistakes.why: The film is the object: the verb takes an ending for it, {{شُفْتُه}}.

practice.tr: The people who came yesterday are nice.

practice.why: The book is the object: {{اشْتَرَيْتُه}} “I bought it”.

practice.q: Your turn: describe two people you know with {{اللِّي}}.

answers.t: أَخُويَا هُوَّ اللِّي بِيُطْبُخ فِي الْبَيْت، وِصَاحِبْتِي هِيَّ اللِّي بِتْسَاعِدْنِي.
answers.r: akhūya huwwa lli biyuṭbukh fi l-bēt, wi-ṣaḥbiti hiyya lli bitsaʿidni.
answers.tr: My brother is the one who cooks at home, and my friend is the one who helps me.

lessons.title: Say what you want, need and must do
lessons.summary: {{عَايِز}} “want”, {{مِحْتَاج}} “need”, {{لَازِم}} “must” and {{نِفْسِي}} “I'd love to”, all with the plain present and no {{أَنْ}}.

goal.t: عَايِز أَتْعَلِّم مَصْرِي، وِلَازِم أَتْكَلِّم كُلّ يَوْم.
goal.r: ʿāyiz atʿallim maṣri, wi-lāzim atkallim kull yōm.
goal.tr: I want to learn Egyptian, and I have to speak every day.

dialog.tr: Do you want to come to the cinema with us?
I'd love to, but I have to study.

blocks.p: MSA says {{أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَذْهَبَ}}. Egyptian drops {{أَنْ}}, and the verb after these words is the plain present, without {{بِـ}}: {{عَايِز أَرُوح|ʿāyiz arūḥ}} I want to go.

{{عَايِز}} is a doer word, so it agrees with whoever wants: {{عَايِز|ʿāyiz}} (a man), {{عَايْزَة|ʿayza}} (a woman), {{عَايْزِين|ʿayzīn}} (a group). It is also written {{عَاوِز}}. Before a noun it means “want” on its own: {{عَايِز شَاي|ʿāyiz shāy}} I want tea.

{{نِفْسِي|nifsi}} is “my self”: {{نِفْسِي أَرُوح}}, “my self (longs) to go”. It takes the other endings too: {{نِفْسَك|nifsak}}, {{نِفْسَهَا|nifsaha}}. “Not”: {{مِش عَايِز}}, {{مِش لَازِم}} (no need), {{مَيِنْفَعْش}} (you can't, it's not allowed).

ex.tr: I (a woman) need to sleep a bit.

practice.q: A friend invites you out, but you're busy. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: Do you want to come with us?
OK, shall we wait for you?

practice.q: A woman says “I need a taxi”. What does she say?
Your turn: say one thing you want to do, one you must do and one you'd love to do.

answers.t: عَايِز أَتْعَشَّى، وِلَازِم أَكَلِّم أُمِّي، وِنِفْسِي أَشُوف الْأَهْرَامَات.
answers.r: ʿāyiz atʿashsha, wi-lāzim akallim ummi, wi-nifsi ashūf il-ahramāt.
answers.tr: I want to have dinner, I have to call my mother, and I'd love to see the pyramids.

lessons.title: Say what there is and isn't
lessons.summary: {{فِيه}} “there is”, {{مَفِيش}} “there isn't”, and {{كَان فِيه}}, {{هَيِكُون فِيه}} for the past and the future.

goal.tr: Is there a pharmacy near here?

dialog.t: لَوْ سَمَحْت، فِيه مَطْعَم كُوَيِّس هِنَا؟
dialog.r: law samaḥt, fī maṭʿam kwayyis hina?
dialog.tr: Excuse me, is there a good restaurant here?

dialog.t: فِيه وَاحِد فِي آخِر الشَّارِع، بَسّ النَّهَارْدَه مَقْفُول.
dialog.r: fī wāḥid fi ākhir ish-shāriʿ, bass in-nahārda maʾfūl.
dialog.tr: There's one at the end of the street, but it's closed today.
There's a fuul cart on the corner!

blocks.p: MSA has {{يُوجَدُ}} and {{هُنَاكَ}}. Egyptian says {{فِيه|fī}} “there is, there are”, and {{مَفِيش|mafīsh}} “there isn't” ({{مَا…ش}} round {{فِيه}}). A question is the same with a rising voice: {{فِيه مَيَّة؟|fī mayya?}} is there any water?

**Before and later**: {{كَان فِيه|kān fī}} there was, {{مَكَانْش فِيه|makansh fī}} there wasn't; {{هَيِكُون فِيه|hayikūn fī}} there will be. {{فِيه}} doesn't change for one or many: {{فِيه نَاس كِتِير|fī nās kitīr}} there are lots of people.

ex.t: كَان فِيه نَاس كِتِير فِي الْحَفْلَة.
ex.r: kān fī nās kitīr fi l-ḥafla.
ex.tr: There were lots of people at the party.

blocks.tip: {{فِيه}} “there is” is spelled like {{فِيه}} “in it”, and Egyptian uses both: {{فِيه سُكَّر فِيه؟}} is there sugar in it?

practice.tr: Yesterday there were lots of people.
Is there a pharmacy near here?

practice.q: You want to know where the pharmacy is. You ask…
Your turn: say what there is and isn't in your street.

answers.t: فِيه سُوبَر مَارْكِت وِقَهْوَة، بَسّ مَفِيش صَيْدَلِيَّة.
answers.r: fī super market wi-ʾahwa, bass mafīsh ṣaydaliyya.
answers.tr: There's a supermarket and a café, but there's no pharmacy.

lessons.title: Count, shop and tell the time
lessons.summary: The numbers lose their endings and change a little ({{تَلَاتَة}}, {{حِدَاشَر}}, {{مِيَّة}}), and the thing counted is simpler than in MSA.
lessons.topic: 1–10 the Cairo way; 11–19 in {{ـتَاشَر}}; {{تَلَات كُتُب}} but {{حِدَاشَر كِتَاب}}; {{بِكَام؟}}

goal.t: عَايِز اتْنَاشَر بَيْضَة، لَوْ سَمَحْت. بِكَام؟
goal.r: ʿāyiz itnāshar bēḍa, law samaḥt. bi-kām?
goal.tr: I'd like twelve eggs, please. How much?

blocks.p: The numbers are the MSA ones without endings, said the Cairo way: {{وَاحِد|wāḥid}}, {{اتْنَيْن|itnēn}}, {{تَلَاتَة|talāta}}, {{أَرْبَعَة|arbaʿa}}, {{خَمْسَة|khamsa}}, {{سِتَّة|sitta}}, {{سَبْعَة|sabʿa}}, {{تَمَانْيَة|tamanya}}, {{تِسْعَة|tisʿa}}, {{عَشَرَة|ʿashara}}.

**3 to 10 before a noun** drop their {{ة}}, and the noun is plural, as in MSA but with no gender rules: {{تَلَات بَنَات|talat banāt}} three girls, {{تَلَات وِلَاد|talat wilād}} three boys. **From 11 up** the noun is singular: {{حِدَاشَر سَنَة|ḥidāshar sana}} eleven years, {{عِشْرِين جِنَيْه|ʿishrīn ginē}} twenty pounds. Units like {{كِيلُو}} and {{جِنَيْه}} often stay singular after any number.
**Prices and time**: {{بِكَام؟|bi-kām?}} how much?; {{السَّاعَة كَام؟|is-sāʿa kām?}} what time is it?; {{السَّاعَة تَلَاتَة وِنُصّ|is-sāʿa talāta w-nuṣṣ}} half past three.

ex.tr: I've got three brothers and sisters.
The shirt is two hundred pounds.

mistakes.why: From 11 up, the noun is singular.
Before a noun, 3 to 10 drop their {{ة}}: {{تَلَات}}.

practice.q: Ask a baker how much the bread ({{الْعَيْش}}) is.
Your turn: say how old you are, and what something you bought cost.

answers.t: عَنْدِي تَلَاتِين سَنَة، وِاشْتَرَيْت جَزْمَة بِخُمْسُمِيَّة جِنَيْه.
answers.r: ʿandi talatīn sana, wi-shtarēt gazma bi-khumsumiyya ginē.
answers.tr: I'm thirty, and I bought a pair of shoes for five hundred pounds.

lessons.title: Say what happens if
lessons.summary: One word for every “if”: {{لَوْ}}. {{لَوْ جِيت بَدْرِي، هَنُخْرُج}} “If you come early, we'll go out.”
lessons.topic: {{لَوْ}} + the past for what may happen; {{لَوْ كُنْت…، كُنْت…}} for what isn't so

goal.t: لَوْ فَاضِي بُكْرَة، تَعَالَى نِتْغَدَّى سَوَا.
goal.r: law fāḍi bukra, taʿāla nitghadda sawa.
goal.tr: If you're free tomorrow, come and have lunch with us.

dialog.t: لَوْ الْجَوّ حِلْو بُكْرَة، نِرُوح الْبَحْر؟
dialog.r: law ig-gaww ḥilw bukra, nirūḥ il-baḥr?
dialog.tr: If the weather's nice tomorrow, shall we go to the beach?

dialog.t: أَكِيد. وِلَوْ مَطَّرِت، نُقْعُد فِي الْبَيْت.
dialog.r: akīd. wi-law maṭṭarit, nuʾʿud fi l-bēt.
dialog.tr: Sure. And if it rains, we'll stay home.

dialog.t: لَوْ كُنْت أَعْرَف، كُنْت جِبْت الْمَايُوه!
dialog.r: law kunt aʿraf, kunt gibt il-mayōh!
dialog.tr: If I'd known, I'd have brought my swimsuit!
There's still time. Bring it tomorrow.

blocks.p: MSA has {{إِذَا}}, {{إِنْ}} and {{لَوْ}}. Egyptian uses {{لَوْ|law}} for all of them. For what may happen, {{لَوْ}} takes the past (or a doer word, an adjective, {{عَنْدَك}}…), and the result takes the future or a command: {{لَوْ جِيت بَدْرِي، هَنُخْرُج|law gīt badri, hanukhrug}} if you come early, we'll go out.
For what isn't so, or wasn't: {{لَوْ كُنْت…|law kunt…}} in the “if” part and {{كُنْت…|kunt…}} in the result: {{لَوْ كُنْت أَعْرَف، كُنْت جِيت|law kunt aʿraf, kunt gīt}} if I'd known, I'd have come.

table: {{لَوْ تَعْبَان، رُوح نَام|law taʿbān, rūḥ nām}}
If you're tired, go to bed.
{{لَوْ كُنْت مَكَانَك، كُنْت قُلْتِلُه|law kunt makānak, kunt ʾultilu}}
If I were you, I'd have told him.

ex.tr: If you want to come, tell me.
If it rains, we won't go out.
If you've got time, come over.
If I'd known, I'd have come.

blocks.tip: {{لَوْ سَمَحْت|law samaḥt}} “if you allow” is how Egyptians say “excuse me” and “please”: {{لَوْ سَمَحْتِي}} to a woman.

mistakes.tr: If you come early, we'll go out.
If I'd known, I'd have come.
mistakes.why: What didn't happen takes {{كُنْت}} in both parts.

practice.tr: If you come early, we'll go out.
If I'd known, I'd have come.
practice.why: What didn't happen: {{كُنْت}} in both parts.

practice.q: A friend makes plans with you. Choose your replies.

lines.tr: If you're free tomorrow, shall we have lunch together?

options: مَاشِي، إِذَا أَنْهَيْتُ مُبَكِّرًا سَأَتَّصِلُ بِكَ.
rs: māshi, idhā anhaytu mubakkiran sa-attaṣilu bik.

lines.why: Asking someone to do something: the command {{اسْتَنَّانِي}} “wait for me”.

practice.q: Say “If you want, come with us” (to a man).
Your turn: say what you'll do tomorrow if the weather is nice, and if it isn't.

answers.t: لَوْ الْجَوّ حِلْو، هَتْمَشَّى عَلَى النِّيل، وِلَوْ مِش حِلْو، هَقْعُد فِي الْبَيْت.
answers.r: law ig-gaww ḥilw, hatmashsha ʿala n-nīl, wi-law mish ḥilw, haʾʿud fi l-bēt.
answers.tr: If the weather's nice, I'll walk along the Nile, and if it isn't, I'll stay home.
